title: Read every story first, and the water you carry
summary: A deliberately light hour with no new C++ in it at all: read both problems all the way through before the editor opens, learn what the grader's coloured boxes will and will not tell you, rehearse the sample test until it is a habit, and plan where the minutes go before the crossing spends them for you.
materials: laptop with Python and the editor, and the usaco.org account a grown-up made last season
the analog desk clock, and no phone on the desk
paper, pencil, and a clipboard or a hard book to lean on
the bug diary and the maker's log
the min-max thermometer outside and the field journal, for the 30 second dawn reading
the wall map, with this weekend's date already under the first sun

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
Before anything else, the shape of this week, said out loud so nobody has to guess at it.

This hour is light on purpose. There is no new C++ in it. The compiler does not get opened today, the Error Bestiary gets nothing new, and nothing gets built. That is not a gap in the plan, it is the plan. Something heavier is happening at the weekend, and a week that piles material on top of it would be a week designed by somebody who was not paying attention.

The design loop, same six moves as always: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix. Today it runs on paper.

Ask: when the morning is fixed and the problems are not, what is actually worth doing in the first ten minutes? Most people open the first problem and start typing. That is a choice, even when nobody notices making it, and this hour is about making it on purpose instead.

Imagine: a crossing morning. It is early, the light is coming up, there is a clock on the desk and it is the only clock in the room. Two problems from a real past contest are open in front of you, both of them read all the way through before a single line got typed. Nobody is going to help. Nobody is going to stop you either.

Plan. Three things this hour, and one of them happens at the weekend.

One, read both stories first, then decide the order and the minutes, on paper, before anything is opened.

Two, the sample test, done properly, rehearsed on a problem you already own so the habit is boring before it is needed.

Three, the crossing itself, on the date you already picked.

About that morning, and two house rules that are bending for it. Both are being said plainly rather than slipped past you.

The first is the clock. This house has never timed your work, on purpose, and it still does not: every peak in Think stays untimed, every problem set stays untimed, the whole summer stays untimed. The crossing mornings are the exception, they are the only exception, and the clock is there because a contest window is a real thing and pretending otherwise would be a worse lesson than the clock is.

The second is the weekend. Weekends have carried nothing all year. Three of them carry a crossing this summer, and no other weekend carries anything at all. Which three they are was settled in week 1, at the map, with the weekends and the dawns yours to pick.

And one rule that does not bend anywhere: the map carries dates and never counts. There is no number on that wall that gets smaller as the summer goes on, and there is not going to be one. You are steering by dates the way you would steer by stars, which is what stars are for.

This weekend's date is already on the wall map, under the first sun, in your own handwriting, because you picked it in week 1. Go and look at it before the hour goes any further. Nothing on the map needs deciding today, and that is the point of it: the date was settled while everything was calm, and this hour is for arriving at it ready.

Five minutes, home row first, then the lines the weekend actually needs. All of this is Python you already own, which is exactly why it is worth drilling: the mornings are lost on punctuation, not on ideas.

For a problem whose page names a file, type each of these five times:

fin = open('mixmilk.in', 'r')
fout = open('mixmilk.out', 'w')
c, m = map(int, fin.readline().split())
print(total, file=fout)
fout.close()

For a problem whose page does not name a file, type each of these five times:

n = int(input())
print(total)

The places hands go wrong: the quote marks around a file name, the comma before the word file, and the brackets closing after split. Land them without looking down.

figure.alt: The grader's coloured boxes and what each letter means. X is a wrong answer: the program ran and lied. T is time limit exceeded: the plan is too slow or a loop never ends. An exclamation mark is a crash or too much memory. E means the output file was empty and M means it was missing altogether, both a right answer delivered to no address. Only a plain green box with no letter means that case came out right.

steps.title: What the grader tells you, and what it refuses to
steps.body:
You have submitted to the USACO grader before and watched the verdict come back. This is what the verdict is actually made of, and more usefully, what it is not.

What it tells you. Your program is run against a set of judging cases, and you get one small coloured box for each of them: green when that case came out right, red when it did not. Every red box carries a letter, and the letters are worth learning by heart because each one rules out a different half of the world.

X means your program finished, printed an answer, and the answer was wrong.

T means it ran out of time on that case.

An exclamation mark means it stopped: it crashed, or it ran out of memory.

E means the output file was empty. M means the output file was missing altogether.

Read that as four different accusations, not four flavours of failure. E and M say the answer went somewhere the grader was not looking, which is almost always a file name typed wrong or a file never written. The exclamation mark says the program fell over, so look for an index that ran off the end of a list, a division by zero, or a line read that was not there. T says the plan is too slow, or a loop never ends. And X says the program ran, finished, printed, and lied. That last one is the mirage, and it is the only letter that tells you nothing about where to look.

One detail that decides how you spend the first hour. The first judging case is usually the same sample that is printed on the problem page, and you have to get that one right before you are told anything at all about the rest. A program that fails the sample buys you no information. Which is the whole argument for the next task in this hour.

What it refuses. It does not show you the input that broke you. It does not point at a line. It does not say why. It will not tell you whether you are close. On the contest's own results page, published afterwards, the test data and a solution are there for anyone to download, and that is a fact about after the morning rather than during it.

And the part worth keeping. The grader does not know your age, your language, how long you worked or how much you wanted it. It reads a file and a clock. That is exactly why a green box from it means something a grown-up saying well done cannot mean.

figure.alt: The heart as a one-way pump: blood flows into a chamber and out through a valve that swings open under pressure, then slams shut the instant blood tries to slosh backward. That is the same one-way rule season 1's LED taught: current, or blood, flows one way through the gate and is blocked completely the other way.

steps.title: The heart is a pump with a one-way rule
steps.body:
Carrying water across the desert this week, imagine the reverse problem: getting water to leave one place, cross a distance, and never accidentally slosh backwards. Your own heart solves that problem every second of your life.

It is a muscular pump, squeezing about 5 litres of blood through your body every minute at rest. That is roughly 100,000 beats in an ordinary day, none of them ordered by you. Between its chambers sit valves, flaps of tissue that swing open one way under pressure and slam shut the instant blood tries to slosh backward.

That is the same rule your season one LED taught you. Current, or blood, flows one way through the gate and is blocked completely the other way. A valve failing to seal is a leak in the pump, the same way a backwards LED blocks a circuit rather than merely dimming it.

Feel your own pulse for fifteen seconds and multiply by four for your resting beats per minute.

steps.title: Read every story first, and decide where the minutes go
steps.body:
Choose the contest. A grown-up opens the past contests list on usaco.org, and you pick a Bronze contest from it and then pick two of its problems. Bronze contests carry three problems, so this is a real choice and it is yours. As an example of the shape rather than a recommendation, the 2018 December Bronze contest held Mixing Milk, The Bucket List and Back and Forth.

One rule about the choosing: do not read the problems to choose them. Choose by contest, take two, and meet them cold. Shopping for easy problems is a habit that costs you exactly the skill this morning is for.

Now the reading, and this is the whole task. Read both problems, all the way through, out loud, before the editor is opened for either of them. All the way through means including the paragraph about where the input comes from and where the answer goes, and including the constraints, the part that says how big the numbers are allowed to get. Those are the two paragraphs everybody skips and they are the two that decide whether your plan is any good.

For each problem, on paper:

Draw it. Farm, buckets, cows, fence, whatever it is. Move things with a pencil until the story is in your hands rather than on the page.

Write the three line plan. What it reads. What it does over and over. What it prints.

Write one line about size. How big can the input get, and roughly how many steps does your plan take at that size? You have owned this move since last season and it belongs here more than anywhere.

Then the part that is new today. Put the two problems in the order you mean to take them, and the order comes from your two plans, not from the order the contest printed them. Beside each one write the number of minutes you intend to spend before you stop and look up. Write it now, while you are calm and nothing is going wrong, because the only version of you who can do this honestly is this one.

That is what reading everything first buys. Ten minutes spent reading is not ten minutes lost from solving. It is the only ten minutes in the morning that can tell you where the other hundred should go.
checklist: Both problems were read out loud, all the way through, including where the input comes from and how big the numbers get
Each problem has a drawing and a three line plan on paper, and both were made before any editor was opened
For each problem I wrote roughly how many steps my plan takes at the largest size the problem allows
The two problems are in the order I mean to take them, and the order came from my plans rather than from the page
Each problem has a number of minutes written beside it, decided now and not in the middle of the morning

steps.title: The sample is a test you already own
steps.body:
Rehearse this on a problem you have already beaten, so that when the weekend comes the whole business is boring. Mixing Milk is the obvious one. If last season's file is still in your folder, open it. If it is not, write it again from the page; it is about fifteen lines and you already know the plan.

First, where the input comes from, which is not the same answer for every problem and must never be guessed. Look at the problem page's own INPUT FORMAT heading, every single time.

Some problems name a file there. Mixing Milk's page says INPUT FORMAT (file mixmilk.in) and OUTPUT FORMAT (file mixmilk.out), and that is exactly what your program has to read and write. Cow Gymnastics names gymnastics.in and gymnastics.out. Most problems from before the December 2020 contest work this way.

From the December 2020 contest onward, USACO switched: input and output are the terminal's, so input() and print() are the whole story and there is no file to make. Both kinds are sitting in the past contests archive right now, so the heading on the page is the only thing that settles it. A perfect program that puts its answer in the wrong place is still rejected, and that is the most ordinary way a good solution dies.

Now the rehearsal, in order.

Copy the SAMPLE INPUT off the problem page into a file of the right name, in the same folder as your program, with nothing added and nothing missing. For Mixing Milk that file is mixmilk.in and it holds three lines: 10 3, then 11 4, then 12 5.

Run your program. Then open the output file it wrote and look. For Mixing Milk it should hold 0, then 10, then 2, which is what the page prints under SAMPLE OUTPUT. The page gives you both halves, so nothing here is a spoiler, it is a rehearsal.

Now compare it properly, because your eye is not good enough for this. A missing newline at the end, or one extra space before a number, is invisible to you and completely visible to the grader. Save the page's sample output into a second file, then compare the two files with a tool.

In PowerShell the tool is fc.exe, and you have to type the .exe, because plain fc in PowerShell is a shortcut for something else entirely and will not compare anything. So: fc.exe mixmilk.out expected.out. When the files match it echoes the two file names and then says FC: no differences encountered, and that last line is the whole verdict. When they differ it prints the offending lines between rows of stars. In Git Bash the tool is diff mixmilk.out expected.out, and diff is the silent kind: a match prints nothing at all. If the two tools ever disagree with each other, it is because Windows and Git Bash end their lines differently, and it is fc.exe that is telling you about the answer rather than about the newlines.

Then do one last thing, which is a trap you will otherwise walk into at seven in the morning. Add a line to your program that prints something extra, anything, then run and compare again. Watch the comparison fail. Then take it out. A debugging print left in the output is a correct program that comes back red, and it is one of the most common ways a solved problem stays unsolved.
checklist: I read the problem page's own INPUT FORMAT heading and said out loud whether this problem uses named files or the terminal
The sample input was copied into a file of exactly the right name, in the same folder as the program
The program ran and I opened what it wrote rather than trusting that it wrote it
The two files were compared with fc.exe or diff, not with my eyes
I added an extra print on purpose, watched the comparison fail, and took it out again

steps.title: The half crossing, and the page you write the day after
steps.body:
This is the weekend brief. Read it now, once, then leave it alone until the morning.

What it is. Two problems from one past Bronze contest, worked in Python, alone, on the real usaco.org grader, at a dawn you picked, with half a contest window on the clock.

How long half a window is. The contest's own page states the window, and a regular USACO contest runs four hours while the US Open runs five. So half a regular Bronze window is two hours. Check the page of the contest you actually picked rather than trusting this sentence.

Why half. Because this is the first one, and a first crossing that is half the distance teaches you almost everything a full one would, including the things you would rather not find out.

What is on the desk. The analog clock, water, paper, a pencil, the laptop. No phone. The clock is on the desk rather than in your head because a clock you have to remember to check is a clock that is checking on you.

Before any of that, the thirty seconds you already own. This is a dawn like every other dawn: read the low, read the high, write them and the date on the next line of the field journal, press reset. Then the desk. That column has been filling since week 1 and week 9 opens it, so a crossing morning is a strange one to leave a hole in.

Who else is there. A grown-up is somewhere in the house, at the door and not in the room. They start nothing, they answer nothing about the problems, and they are not watching you work. They are there for the reason a belayer stands at the bottom of a climb, which is not to climb it.

Breaks are yours to call, whenever you want, for as long as you want. The clock keeps running through them, because that is what a window is, and knowing that is exactly why the decision to take one is worth making rather than avoiding.

One rule, and it is the only one that could spoil the morning. The contest's results page publishes its test data and a written solution. Do not open either of them until the morning is over and the report is written. A crossing where you looked at the map is not a crossing, it is a walk.

What counts as reaching the summit. Not a green box. A green box is lovely and it is not the measurement. What counts is a morning you can describe honestly afterwards. A rejection you debugged and understood is a summit reached in weather, and the weather is worth more in the log than a clear day would have been.

The day after, not the same day, write the report. It is the form you learned in week 3 and it has not changed: route, then weather, then exactly one pack item, and never a score. One thing is added this time, and only one. Beside each item on the route, write the minutes. What time you started reading. What time the first line got typed. What time you submitted. What time you parked something. You will not remember those the following week and week 8 wants them, because in week 8 you are going to put your remembered morning next to your measured morning and see how far apart they were.
checklist: The date and the dawn are mine, they are on the wall map as a date, and nobody moved them for me
The analog clock was the only clock in the room, and the phone was somewhere else in the house
Two problems from one past Bronze contest, in Python, alone, submitted to the real grader
The contest's published solutions and test data stayed shut until after the report was written
The report was written the day after, as route, weather and one pack item, with the minutes written beside the route

steps.title: Bug diary, and the water you carry
steps.body:
The bug diary has no compiler in it this week, because nothing got compiled. This week's chapter is a different list: the ways a right plan still comes back red.

Write these three in now, before the weekend, as a page you can glance at rather than a lesson you have to remember. The letters they come back as are already on this hour's science page, so the diary only needs the mistake itself.

The file name is wrong, or the capital letters are. mixmilk.in is not MixMilk.in.

A debugging print was left in the output, so a program that was right came back red.

One line too few or one line too many was read from the input, usually because the first line says how many lines follow and it got counted as one of them.

Then the last thing in the hour, and it is about the clock rather than the code.

A window is not a judge. It is a canteen. When you set out across something exposed you do not carry all the water you would like, you carry what you can carry, and the skill is not drinking less, it is deciding in advance where you will drink. That is why the minutes got written beside each problem on paper this morning while everything was calm.

So minutes spent on a problem you then park are not wasted minutes. They bought you a real thing: the knowledge that it is the harder one, which is information you did not have when you sat down. Parking is a move, not a surrender.

And the sentence to take to the desk on the morning. A clock measures a morning. It does not measure you. Those are two different jobs and the clock is only qualified for one of them.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photograph the two paper plans from this hour: the drawings, the three line plans, the size lines, the order you chose and the minutes written beside each problem. Then the sample rehearsal: the input file you made, what your program wrote, and what the comparison tool printed when the two files matched and again when the extra print was in. Then a photo of the wall map with this weekend's date under the first sun, in your own handwriting. After the weekend, add the report page you wrote the day after, with the minutes down the side of the route.
